BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: An upper level ridge will remain over the area on Thursday with strong southwest flow aloft with multiple low pressure systems offshore in the Gulf of Alaska. This will keep temperatures well above normal through Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light rain and high mountain snow showers tonight. Mostly cloudy but dry in southern areas.
- Warm and dry Wednesday and Thursday. Near record high temperatures.
- Chance of precipitation Friday night and Saturday. Colder with rain and snow next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Weak Pacific cold front will bring light rain to northern zones tonight, ending before sunrise. Total precipitation will be .10 inch at most. Southern zones will be cloudy but dry. Clouds will limit overnight cooling. Tuesday will become sunny in southern zones but remain mostly cloudy in the north as a weak following warm front passes through. Wednesday looks mostly sunny, breezy, and warm as an upper ridge amplifies over the interior western US while a trough deepens in the eastern Pacific. Southeasterly surface winds will increase to 15 to 25 mph, and with skies becoming mostly sunny, high temps both Wednesday and Thursday will be 65 to 72 degrees in southern valleys, near record highs for those days.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper level ridge will remain over the area on Thursday with strong southwest flow aloft with multiple low pressure systems offshore in the Gulf of Alaska. This will keep temperatures well above normal through Friday. Temperatures will be near record highs Thursday and Friday with breezy to windy conditions. A cold front will approach the area on Friday. Gusts 35-50 mph are possible on Friday across the open terrain of southeast Oregon with gusts 20-40 mph elsewhere. Still high uncertainty on the timing of the cold front, with differences up to 12 to 24 hours, but showers increase across the area late Friday night into Saturday. There is significant differences in the models Saturday and beyond, but conditions are favoring cooler and unsettled late in the weekend with mountain snows early next week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Ensemble guidance does favor a weak system moving through the region over the weekend. This will give us our first chance in a while for mountain rain/snow showers. Accumulations look light at this point, given the lack of decent moisture and strong forcing.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will likely prevail through Friday.
- Increasing chances for light mountain rain/snow showers by this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Our weather pattern this week will be dominated by a persistent upper level ridge over the western United States. This will keep our forecast area dry with above normal temperatures through Friday. By this weekend, a weak system could bring light precipitation (30-40% chance as of now) to the high country and cooler temperatures to the region.

Current water vapor satellite imagery shows a weak upper level shortwave over the far Pacific Northwest. This will trek across the northern United States and into the northern Great Plains Tuesday and into Wednesday. While this system will be too far away from Colorado for any precipitation chances, there will be increased cloud cover over our region on Tuesday, which should keep temperatures over the Denver area a few degrees cooler than Monday. However, still expect maximum temperatures to be in the mid-to-high 60s across the plains. A "cool" front (if you can even call it that) associated with the system will bring breezy winds to the northern and eastern plains, with gusts up to 20-30 mph possible in the afternoon. Due to this, elevated fire weather conditions will be possible. However, relative humidity values should stay above critical thresholds, especially with the expected cloud cover.

We will be a bit cooler on Wednesday, with highs in the low-to-mid 60s. But, this will be short-lived as the axis of the upper level ridge should shift over wester Colorado on Thursday and Friday. Temperatures in the mid-to-high 60s will return, with a few ensemble solutions showing low 70s.

Ensemble guidance does favor a weak system moving through the region over the weekend. This will give us our first chance in a while for mountain rain/snow showers. Accumulations look light at this point, given the lack of decent moisture and strong forcing. For the plains, precipitation chances do not look as favorable over the weekend. However, there could be an isolated rain shower or two. We should begin cooling down towards the beginning of next week, with seasonal temperatures returning and possibly a more active pattern. Stay tuned...

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday-Monday...West to southwest flow aloft prevails, and with minimal low and mid level moisture, chances for precipitation will be limited. Maximum temperatures will be similar each day, from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue into and through the end of the week.
- Windy conditions are expected Tuesday, however, critical fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Benign weather continues in the short term with mostly sunny skies and mild temperatures expected for the remainder of Monday afternoon. Quiet conditions will carry on into the overnight hours, with low temperatures once again staying on the mild side for early November.

The weather gets *slightly* more exciting on Tuesday. A dry upper- level shortwave will move into the CWA from the northwest bringing with it wind and some cloud cover. MSLP gradients will tighten along and west of the Laramie Range, helping to increase winds aloft. 800 to 700 mb winds will max out around 40 kts with decent subsidence over the typical wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming. Gusts up to 50 MPH can be expected, with an occasional gust to 55 MPH possible. In-house guidance gives about a 40 percent chance of high winds at Arlington, Bordeaux, and the South Laramie Range, however, marginal events like this tend not to verify in El Nino conditions. The shortwave will also bring increased cloud cover, likely in the form of high clouds and some mountain waves from strong winds. The windy conditions will also lead to a warm day across the eastern half of the CWA. Downsloping winds will help raise temperatures into the 60s and low 70s, which is about 10 to 15 degrees above average for this time of year. Winds will ease during the evening hours, once again leading to quiet overnight conditions.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday...Dry northwest flow aloft prevails, with slightly cooler temperatures compared to Tuesday based on 700 mb temperatures. Breezy to windy conditions based on the low and mid level gradients.
Thursday...As a ridge aloft moves further eastward across Wyoming and 700 mb temperatures rise to near 6 Celsius, a warming trend will begin with high temperatures from the upper 50s to upper 60s.
Friday...Ridging aloft moves overhead centered from western North Dakota to eastern Colorado, with maximum temperatures similar to those of Thursday.

Saturday...A progressive negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft moves into western Wyoming, spreading increasing mid and high level cloudiness across our counties, with low POPS across southern Carbon County, for rain and snow showers, including the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Slightly cooler with the increase in cloud cover.

Sunday-Monday...West to southwest flow aloft prevails, and with minimal low and mid level moisture, chances for precipitation will be limited. Maximum temperatures will be similar each day, from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Models indicate a deep trough developing off the West Coast by the end of the week, which has the potential to bring a shift to cooler and wetter conditions over eastern Utah and western Colorado for the coming weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures will continue through the work week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure will persist through the week, bringing warmer and drier conditions. Temperatures are expected to run 5-10 degrees above normal through at least Friday, with mostly clear skies. A quick moving system to our north will bring increased cloud cover on Tuesday afternoon, as well as maybe some breezy winds across northeast Utah and northwest Colorado. Otherwise, expect sunny skies and light winds.

Models indicate a deep trough developing off the West Coast by the end of the week, which has the potential to bring a shift to cooler and wetter conditions over eastern Utah and western Colorado for the coming weekend. Model agreement remains poor this far out, so be sure to stay tuned to see how the forecast develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Thursday through Sunday...upper level high pressure will rebuild across Colorado for Thursday into Saturday, with continued dry weather.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued dry and mild into next weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...high pressure continues to dominate the region with quiet weather in place. Satellite and radar imagery are clear, and temperatures are in the 60s across the Plains. Temperatures will continue to warm, with upper 60s to lower 70s this afternoon.

Tonight through Tuesday night...high pressure continues with dry weather continuing. Low temperatures tonight will fall 30s across the Plains, and 20s for the San Luis Valley. High temperatures on Tuesday will warm back into the upper 60s to mid 70s on the Plains, and near 60 for the San Luis Valley.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Models and ensemble guidance remain in good agreement through the extended period, with the all guidance trending south with a system next weekend.

Wednesday...a dry cold front will drop south across the Plains during the morning hours, causing a northerly wind shift by mid morning. A few gusts near 25 mph may be possible near the Kansas border through the afternoon. The main impact from the front will be slightly cooler temperatures, with 60s across the Plains.

Thursday through Sunday...upper level high pressure will rebuild across Colorado for Thursday into Saturday, with continued dry weather. Temperatures will warm nicely, with upper 60s to lower 70s during this period, and overnight lows in the 30s on the Plains and 20s across the San Luis Valley. As mentioned above, guidance has tended south with an upper trough moving into the region. Current guidance takes the upper wave across northern Mexico, and keeps southern Colorado dry. NBM guidance has yet to catch up to the rest of the guidance and has low pops over the weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Global deterministic models are in fairly good agreement bringing the next trough into the area for Saturday. This progressive system would bring a quick shot of widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild conditions will persist areawide through a majority of the week, with the next chance for precipitation arriving this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad ridge over the area today will give way to a weak shortwave trough that is currently rippling through the PacNW and western Nevada. Some high clouds will continue to cross Utah ahead of it, otherwise little moisture will be available as this trough crosses Utah Tuesday morning. Main impact will be some cold advection on Tuesday under a northwesterly flow. While temperatures in the valleys will cool slightly, stronger cooling aloft should weaken the inversions in place, clearing out some of the valley haze. After the trough exits the area, a strong ridge will return to the area Tuesday night through late week.

Global deterministic models are in fairly good agreement bringing the next trough into the area for Saturday. This progressive system would bring a quick shot of widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the area. However, cluster analysis of global ensembles show a 50/50 split between this wet solution and a drier solution where the trough remains well offshore.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. You may encounter wet, loose avalanches on steep south and southwest aspects in the afternoon, particularly near rock outcrops.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, holding too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow features if you find them below ridges or in deeper gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches. On isolated slopes at higher elevations, you might encounter stiffer slabs over weak layers 1 to 2 feet deep on the north side of the compass. Look for stiffer snow surfaces or rounded drifts below ridges or deeper gullies as features to avoid, especially in steep, consequential terrain.
